RESILAGENT: A Three-Pillar Architecture for Cyber-Physical Resilience in Electrical Power and Energy Systems

Nikolaos Kekatos1, Georgios Koutidis1, Konstantinos Antonakopoulos2, Stylianos Basagiannis3,
Sokratis Katsikas4, Georgios Kavallieratos4, Alexios Lekidis5, Tom Nianios1, Elpiniki Papageorgiou5 Affiliation:  1Clone Systems, Cyprus  –  {nkekatos, gkoutidis, tnianios}@clone-systems.com 2BITREZUS, Greece  –  ka@bitrezus.com 3IHU, Greece  –  basagiannis@ihu.gr 4NTNU, Norway  –  {sokratis.katsikas, georgios.kavallieratos}@ntnu.no 5UTH, Greece  –  {alekidis, elpinikipapageorgiou}@uth.gr
Abstract

Electrical Power and Energy Systems face hybrid threats that combine cyber intrusions, physical sabotage and climate-driven stress, and routinely outpace today’s siloed monitoring stacks. We present RESILAGENT, a concept architecture organised around three operational pillars, Sensing & Data Intelligence, Resilience Analytics & Reporting, and Incident Response & Recovery, mediated by a Cloud-based Orchestrator and exercised through a closed Detect-Simulate-Decide-Sign loop. The framework fuses agentic artificial intelligence and multimodal large language models for cross-modal detection, real-time digital twins for what-if simulation, and a permissioned blockchain anchor for tamper-evident threat intelligence and CER/NIS2-aligned evidence. We instantiate it on two scenarios, a transmission operator under coordinated cyber compromise, sabotage and heatwave, and a distribution operator under a supply-chain compromise during a storm, and report an IEEE-bus micro-benchmark that quantifies each pillar through false-data-injection attack detection, cyber–physical fusion lift, N-1 contingency screening and anchor cost.

Index Terms: 
critical infrastructure resilience, agentic AI, digital twin, large language models, blockchain, smart grid security, hybrid threats, NIS2.

I Introduction

The cyber-physical exposure of Electrical Power and Energy Systems (EPES) is widening. The European Union Agency for Cybersecurity again ranks energy among the most targeted Union verticals [2, 3], and a decade of incidents, BlackEnergy / Industroyer against the Ukrainian grid (2015–2016), Industroyer2 (2022), Colonial Pipeline (2021), the Viasat KA-SAT wiper (2022), and growing supply-chain advisories on solar inverters and Distributed Energy Resource (DER) firmware [1], confirms the threat is no longer hypothetical, while heatwaves, storms and floods overlap with it to produce compound disruptions beyond any single tool. Yet operators still run siloed stacks: commercial Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) and Intrusion Detection System (IDS) appliances for cyber, Closed-Circuit Television (CCTV) and access control for physical security, hydro-meteorological feeds for environment, and manual standard-operating-procedure escalation. Cyber alerts never reach the dispatch console, weather warnings never reach the Security Operations Centre (SOC), and Critical Entities Resilience (CER, Directive (EU) 2022/2557) [5] and Network and Information Security (NIS2, Directive (EU) 2022/2555) [4] evidence is still curated in spreadsheets, widening the Mean-Time-To-Detect / Mean-Time-To-Respond (MTTD/MTTR) gap exactly when the attacker compounds the incident.

Contributions. This position paper introduces RESILAGENT, a staged three-pillar architecture for EPES resilience that integrates multimodal agentic detection, Digital-Twin (DT) contingency analysis and tamper-evident evidence generation, and validates the minimum viable stack through an IEEE-bus micro-benchmark. No closed-loop grid control originates from a Large Language Model (LLM) in this design: high-impact actions require explicit operator confirmation and pass a DT plausibility filter first. The specific contributions are:

  1. 1.

    A three-pillar architecture, Sensing & Data Intelligence, Resilience Analytics & Reporting, Incident Response & Recovery, mediated by a Cloud-based Orchestrator and tied to an eight-stage closed-loop workflow.

  2. 2.

    A technology-coherent design in which agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI)/multimodal LLMs serve detection, Digital Twins serve simulation/decision, and a permissioned blockchain anchors every artefact for CER/NIS2 evidence by construction.

  3. 3.

    An EPES use-case instantiation on two parallel EU pilots, a national Transmission System Operator (TSO) under coordinated cyber & sabotage & heatwave, and a Distribution System Operator (DSO) under DER firmware compromise & storm, with explicit per-step technology mapping.

  4. 4.

    An IEEE-bus micro-benchmark that quantifies the contribution of each pillar on the IEEE 14/30/118-bus cases: physics-aware False Data Injection Attack (FDIA) detection, cyber–physical fusion lift, DT-driven N−1N{-}1 contingency screening, and blockchain anchor cost.

Section II surveys the state of the art; Section III details the RESILAGENT three-pillar architecture and the closed-loop workflow; Section IV presents the TSO and DSO application scenarios; Section V reports the evaluation roadmap and the initial micro-benchmark; Section VI analyses open challenges; Section VII concludes.

II State of the Art

AI-powered detection in EPES. Classical multivariate IDS for smart grids, ARIES [6] and SPEAR SIEM [7], outperform commercial appliances but are offline and single-modality; the 2024–2025 wave added graph-attention / Kolmogorov–Arnold detectors on Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) topology [8], LLM-based relay detectors above 97 % [9], and explainable LLM frameworks for Automatic Generation Control anomalies [10, 11]; recent work also targets best-practice cyber training for power-grid operators [25], but operationalising any at fleet scale remains open [3]. Agentic AI and digital twins. Agentic AI, autonomous LLM-backed agents with tools, memory and planning, has entered CISA practitioner guidance on careful adoption [12] and secure AI in operational technology [13], with Farid [14] grounding decentralised post-disruption reconfiguration; for simulation, Eckhart and Ekelhart [16] survey DTs as a Cyber-Physical-System (CPS) security primitive and Saad et al. [15] build an IoT-based DT for microgrid resilience, yet none expose the DT to an agent layer issuing what-if queries during a live hybrid event, the coupling RESILAGENT targets. Blockchain CTI and data spaces. CTI-sharing surveys flag integrity, attribution and trust as the persistent gaps [18, 17, 7], motivating blockchain-anchored designs and the International Data Spaces energy framework [19] that positions Gaia-X / IDS connectors as NIS2-aligned CTI infrastructure, while production still relies on best-effort MISP exchanges that miss the CER/NIS2 audit trail. EU R&D lineage. Despite a decade of EU R&D across smart-grid security (SDN-microSENSE, ELECTRON, CyberSEAS), power-grid resilience and data spaces (eFORT, R2D2, ENERSHARE), cyber-physical CI resilience (PRECINCT, ATLANTIS) and CI cybersecurity with AI (DYNABIC, AI4CYBER), no operational architecture closes the loop between agentic detection, digital-twin analysis and verifiable evidence generation while preserving CER/NIS2 compliance and human approval for high-impact actions, the gap RESILAGENT targets.

Positioning of the Contribution

Table I positions RESILAGENT against the closest 2024–2026 comparables across seven coverage dimensions: none of them simultaneously covers all seven, the gap RESILAGENT targets as an advanced proof-of-concept exercised end-to-end (Section V) on two EPES scenarios (Section IV).

III RESILAGENT Three-Pillar Architecture

We use three terms precisely. An agent is an LLM-backed component with tools, memory and a planner; modality-specific agents emit anomalies and a multimodal fusion agent consolidates them into one hybrid-event hypothesis driving a Security Orchestration, Automation and Response (SOAR) playbook under a human-in-the-loop checkpoint. A real-time Digital Twin is a continuously synchronised simulation of grid topology, loads, generation and protection settings, exposed as a DT-as-a-Service (DTaaS) endpoint and coupled to cyber emulators via co-simulation (HELICS [23], OPAL-RT Hardware-in-the-Loop, HIL); it is at once the “normal” reference frame, a forward-prediction engine and a counterfactual sandbox [26]. A blockchain anchor is a permissioned ledger (Hyperledger Fabric) binding every artefact, detector output, DT contingency, SOAR action and Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) bundle to a tamper-evident hash chain; it has no detection role, contributing verifiability, supply-chain attribution and CER/NIS2 evidence by construction.

Figure 1 shows the three pillars mediated by the Cloud-based Orchestrator; Figure 2 deepens this into the experimental pipeline exercised by the micro-benchmark (Section V) and the two pilots (Section IV).

III-A Minimum Viable Stack

Only four technologies are irreducible for a first deployment: (i) a multi-modal monitoring agent with at least one cyber and one physical input (P1); (ii) a real-time Digital Twin supplying the residual / contingency reference frame (P2); (iii) an LLM-backed fusion / playbook agent binding heterogeneous inputs into explainable actions (P1→\toP3); and (iv) a blockchain anchor signing every detection, simulation and action (P3). Removing any one breaks the loop. Every other technology in Fig. 1, vision-LLM, federated learning, EWS, blockchain-anchored CTI, service/data migration, compliance automation, AI risk scoring, is a stageable extension; we recommend the four-core stack on a single-sector pilot first, then extensions as operator maturity and regulatory pressure require.

III-B The Three Pillars and the Orchestrator

P1, Sensing & Data Intelligence. Modality-specific agents observe SCADA, Phasor Measurement Unit (PMU), video, acoustic, vibration and environmental Early-Warning-System (EWS) sensors [8, 9]; novelty detection targets zero-day patterns; a multimodal LLM fusion agent binds anomalies sharing site, time or asset into hybrid-event hypotheses [11]; federated learning improves detection across operators without sharing raw data [19]; and a blockchain-secured CTI plane enables tamper-evident peer exchange under the STIX/TAXII standards [18, 17, 7]. P2, Resilience Analytics & Reporting. A DTaaS layer (INTO-CPS) [24] hosts high-fidelity grid twins for predictive simulation and stress testing [16]; co-simulation supports real-time cyber-physical reconfiguration [15, 23, 27]; multi-hazard simulation combines cyber, physical and environmental stressors; AI-driven risk assessment evaluates cascading impacts; and dashboards consolidate recommendations, on an open stack of pandapower [22], HELICS and OPAL-RT (HIL). P3, Incident Response & Recovery. Once P2 ranks mitigations, P3 runs AI-assisted forensics and adaptive containment, LLM-based explainable playbooks [10], survivability via hot standby, automated failover and intentional islanding, immutable blockchain audit [18], and CER/NIS2 compliance automation [5, 4]. Orchestrator. A Cloud-based Orchestrator presents a unified SOC / Network Operations Centre (NOC) / Energy Control Room view, ranks P2 mitigations, automates low-risk SOAR responses, escalates to civil-protection authorities, and signs every action and CTI artefact in a blockchain-anchored evidence vault [4, 5].

III-C Closed-Loop Resilience Workflow

At runtime the pillars interact through a single closed loop, the eight stages drawn in Fig. 2 and closed by the dashed return arrow of Fig. 1: Observe (P1) detects and correlates per-modality anomalies; Simulate & Decide (P2) explores contingency paths on the live DT and returns a ranked, confidence-scored mitigation list; Act & Adapt (P3) executes low-risk actions through SOAR while high-risk actions await operator confirmation, then learns, emitting a blockchain-anchored CER/NIS2 evidence package that feeds both the next cycle and external auditors.

III-D Deployment View

Fig. 3 maps the framework onto three tiers: a distributed edge that keeps raw SCADA on-premise (sensing agents, a DT-residual detector, a blockchain peer with optional local LLM); a centralised operator cloud / SOC hosting the Orchestrator, fusion agent, DTaaS, SOAR and the single human-in-the-loop checkpoint; and a federated tier sharing only model updates and signed CTI over the permissioned ledger. Edge-to-cloud traffic uses TLS-secured Kafka/Flink and gRPC; cloud-to-data-space an International-Data-Spaces / Gaia-X connector.

IV EPES Application Scenarios

We ground the framework in two pilot scenarios, a national TSO and a regional DSO, each illustrating one stress mode; every pilot step maps to a result of Section V.

IV-A TSO Scenario: Cyber Intrusion under a Heatwave

A national TSO with >9 000{>}9\,000 km of high-voltage lines and ENTSO-E interconnections faces a coordinated hybrid campaign during a 42 ∘C summer peak that combines (i) credential compromise on a SCADA VPN gateway, (ii) deliberate damage at a 400 kV transformer substation, and (iii) a heatwave reducing hydro output by 40 %. Under RESILAGENT, P1 fuses an Operational-Technology (OT) flow anomaly (R1–R3-class), a vision-LLM signal on substation CCTV and a Sentinel-2 tile, and an EWS heatwave alert into one hypothesis; P2 runs the N−1N{-}1 contingency on a Common-Information-Model network in pandapower (R4-class), finding that severing one 400 kV line overloads two parallel ones; P3 emits an LLM SOAR playbook (R6-class) proposing load shedding, genset dispatch and VPN-segment isolation, all signed by the anchor (R5).

IV-B DSO Scenario: DER Supply-Chain Compromise under a Storm

A regional DSO with growing DER penetration is exposed to a sector-wide supply-chain risk on DER firmware [1, 2]. A malicious update is silently installed on a cluster of solar inverters months before an Atlantic storm; at landfall, wind brings down feeders and the implant triggers, disconnecting tens of megawatts of inverter capacity. Under RESILAGENT, the EWS agent pre-stages the DT with the storm trajectory; a firmware-attestation agent hashes fielded firmware against the blockchain-anchored vendor-advisory ledger [18] and flags the malicious version before it fires; at impact, the fusion agent combines storm position, mass inverter dropout (SCADA/DER telemetry) and post-event imagery from a vision-LLM damage classifier; the DT re-runs with the updated topology (R4-class) and the P3 agent (R6-class) islands the segment serving a hospital and shelter, every step bound to the same SHA-256 chain (R5) producing the CER/NIS2 evidence package [5, 4].

V Evaluation Roadmap

V-A Open-Source Toolchain and Datasets

RESILAGENT is being prototyped on an open-source stack: pandapower [22] for the static power-flow DT; HELICS [23] for cyber–physical co-simulation; OPAL-RT for HIL where licensed; Apache Kafka/Flink for the ingestion plane; Suricata, Zeek and Wazuh for cyber sensing; LangGraph for the agent layer with locally hosted LLMs (Llama-3, Mistral) for sovereignty; and Hyperledger Fabric for the trust anchor. Planned benchmark datasets include PNNL Electricity/Gas IDS, HAI 22.04, iTrust EPIC, ENTSO-E Transparency, OEDI outage events and Copernicus EWS feeds.

V-B Metrics

Beyond detection statistics (F1, precision, recall, per modality and fused), the project will report MTTD and MTTR, service-continuity (kW and critical-load fraction restored), operator burden (analyst-minutes per incident), a composite resilience index over severity, duration and recovery, and compliance latency from incident onset to a NIS2-compliant evidence package [4].

V-C Initial Micro-Benchmark

Setup

All experiments run on a 2024 Apple-silicon laptop (Python 3.9, pandapower 3.2.2), complete in under five minutes on deterministic seeds, and total roughly 500 lines of Python. The IEEE 14-, 30- and 118-bus cases [22] provide the grid models; for each snapshot we jitter every load by ±25%\pm 25\,\%, solve AC power flow to obtain the true bus-voltage vector 𝐱\mathbf{x}, and synthesise the measurement vector 𝐳=𝐱+𝒩⁡(0,σ2)\mathbf{z}=\mathbf{x}+\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}), where 𝒩⁡(0,σ2)\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}) denotes zero-mean Gaussian noise with standard deviation σ=0.01\sigma{=}0.01 in per-unit (p.u.). FDIA samples add an offset drawn from the continuous uniform distribution 𝒰⁡[α−1,α+1]​σ\mathcal{U}[\alpha{-}1,\alpha{+}1]\,\sigma on kk randomly chosen buses, where the stealth parameter α\alpha scales the injection (a smaller α\alpha is stealthier) and kk is the number of attacked buses. We contrast three detectors that stand in for three architectural choices: an unsupervised Isolation Forest (no labels, no physics); a Logistic Regression on residual statistics (the max\max, mean and standard deviation of the residuals rir_{i}, and the count of |ri|>3|r_{i}|{>}3, where rir_{i} is the per-bus measurement residual) modelling the physics-aware signal a P1 agent extracts via the DT; and a small Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) on the raw measurement vector, modelling a feature-blind end-to-end neural detector.

Scope

The benchmark is intentionally a proxy evaluation: it does not claim to validate a national TSO or DSO deployment. Each experiment isolates one mechanism required by the proposed architecture (physics-aware detection, cyber–physical feature fusion, DT contingency screening, cryptographic anchoring, and orchestration latency); the cyber feature, the vision input and the production ledger are deliberately replaced by lightweight proxies. Detection and fusion (Results 1–3) are reported on the IEEE 14-bus case, while DT contingency screening (Result 4) and anchor cost (Result 5) extend directly to the 30- and 118-bus networks; a full multi-case characterisation of detection and fusion across all three networks is the immediate next step.

Pillar 1, Result 1: nominal operating point

At α=2​σ\alpha{=}2\sigma on two random buses (800 snapshots), the residual-aware Logistic Regression reaches an Area Under the Receiver-Operating-Characteristic Curve (AUC) =0.82=0.82, the unsupervised Isolation Forest AUC =0.75=0.75, and the feature-blind MLP collapses to AUC =0.61=0.61 (Fig. 4(a)). Median per-sample latency (Fig. 4(b)) is 48 μ\mus (LogReg), 43 μ\mus (MLP) and 4.5 ms (Isolation Forest), all within sub-second control-loop budgets. The DT-derived zz-scored residuals carry the inductive bias a feature-blind network cannot learn at this sample size.

Pillar 1, Result 2: stealth boundary

Sweeping α∈[1,5]​σ\alpha\in[1,5]\sigma over three seeds (Fig. 4(c)), the residual-aware detector dominates everywhere and reaches AUC ≥0.95\geq 0.95 from α≥3​σ\alpha{\geq}3\sigma, while the MLP fails in the stealth regime (AUC 0.540.54 at α=1​σ\alpha{=}1\sigma) and only catches up at α≥4​σ\alpha{\geq}4\sigma where a human is likely to notice anyway. The gap is widest where the signal is weakest, the practically relevant regime for advanced adversaries.

Pillar 1, Result 3: cyber–physical fusion

With a synthetic 1-D “SCADA write-rate” feature (Gaussian-shifted by ∼0.7​σ{\sim}0.7\sigma under attack) and Logistic Regression over five seeds (1 200 snapshots), AUCs are physics-only 0.807±0.0110.807\pm 0.011, cyber-only 0.675±0.0330.675\pm 0.033, fused 0.838±0.003\mathbf{0.838\pm 0.003} (Fig. 4(d)). Fusion lifts AUC by 3.1 pp over physics-only and 16.3 pp over cyber-only, and the seed-to-seed standard deviation drops by an order of magnitude. That stability is the empirical case for the multimodal fusion agent at the heart of P1.

Pillar 2, Result 4: Digital-Twin contingency screening

On IEEE 14-bus at 1.25×1.25\times peak load the DT enumerates all 15 N−1N{-}1 contingencies in ∼250\sim 250 ms; none exceeds the 100 % rating (Fig. 5(a)). The loadings are mild on this generously rated case; the point is that a complete sub-second N−1N{-}1 audit turns an annual offline study into a live dashboard, the quantitative ground that lets P3 propose pre-emptive load shedding rather than react to a trip.

Pillar 3, Result 5: blockchain anchor cost

We stream 20 000 synthetic incident events (each carrying a 32-byte payload hash, operator id, type and timestamp) through three signing schemes implemented with Python hashlib: a per-event SHA-256 leaf, an append to a linear chain, and a Merkle tree over the whole window. Averaged cost per event is 1.20 μ\mus (SHA-256 leaf), 0.26 μ\mus (chain append) and 0.35 μ\mus (Merkle root) (Fig. 5(b)), three orders of magnitude below the detector latency (∼50​μ{\sim}50\,\mus) and four below the DT solve (∼16{\sim}16 ms): local anchoring is negligible at the control-loop budget. A production permissioned ledger (Hyperledger Fabric) would add millisecond-range ordering, endorsement and commit latency, which remains deployment-dependent.

Result 6: end-to-end pipeline

To show the components compose, we chain all tools in a single-incident script: a live Open-Meteo EWS fetch, the IEEE 14-bus DT N−1N{-}1 audit triggered by the EWS regime label, the FDIA detector of Results 1–3, a vision stub, a local Llama-3.2 agent emitting a JSON action plan, and a SHA-256 chain anchoring every step. The agent labelled the regime STORM, the DT cleared the network as N−1N{-}1-secure, and the agent emitted an ordered high-severity plan (12.8 s), anchored to a deterministic root. We deliberately separate proxy artefacts from deployment estimates: the 255 s wall-clock is dominated by a benchmark detector that retrains from scratch (the 237 s Detector bar, Fig. 5(c)), absent in deployment where inference is the 50 μ\mus of Result 1. The deployment-representative path, the DT N−1N{-}1 audit (∼250{\sim}250 ms), the Llama-3.2 rationale (12.8 s) and microsecond-scale detection and anchoring, gives an effective LLM & DT decision latency of ∼17{\sim}17 s, wrong for protection-relay loops but right for the human-in-the-loop stage the framework targets.

V-D Federated Learning and Continuous Risk

Federated learning across operators

Federated learning (FL) is the mechanism by which detection improves across the European fleet without raw data ever leaving an operator, directly serving the data-residency obligations of NIS2 and the EU data-space lineage [19] (e.g. ENERSHARE). Each TSO/DSO trains the multimodal anomaly model locally and shares only model updates; a secure-aggregation round (FedAvg-style) at the centralised aggregator of Tier B (Fig. 3) combines them into a new global model. Because the threat landscape is shared but telemetry is not, FL lets a stealth-FDIA pattern seen by one operator harden every peer’s detector while each keeps its SCADA on-premise. The open risk is model poisoning by a compromised participant or sensor; RESILAGENT mitigates it by signing every update and anchoring the round on the trust ledger (Result 5), so a poisoned contribution is attributable and revocable, and by DT-based plausibility filtering of the aggregated model. A quantitative FL evaluation, convergence and poisoning robustness across operators, is a primary item on the pilot roadmap.

Continuous risk and resilient operations

RESILAGENT replaces the annual-audit posture with a per-event loop that re-scores threat likelihood (P1), impact (DT N−1N{-}1/N−2N{-}2, Result 4) and residual mitigation risk continuously. A Governance, Risk and Compliance cockpit maps every artefact to CER and NIS2 controls [4, 5], and the anchor (Result 5) makes the chain externally verifiable, dropping prototype evidence generation to seconds. Supply-chain and AI-model risk, the blind spot of cyber-only frameworks, is covered by firmware attestation against the anchored vendor-advisory ledger (DSO pilot) and the signed FL updates above.

VI Open Challenges

Trust, explainability and real-time performance. Operators will not accept agent escalations they cannot interrogate, and EPES control loops are sub-second while large LLM inference is not. RESILAGENT pairs every recommendation with a DT-derived rationale (Result 4) and a signed evidence trail, and tiers compute: distilled models on the hot path (μ\mus-scale, Results 1–3), the DT for what-if (∼250{\sim}250 ms), and larger LLMs for explanation. Open problems are calibrated uncertainty under distribution shift and the maximum LLM size within a ≤250{\leq}250 ms playbook budget.

Legacy OT, adversarial sensors and post-quantum crypto. IEC 60870-5-104, DNP3, Modbus and proprietary SCADA must be observed non-intrusively via out-of-band taps and network slicing. A compromised PMU or camera, or an FL poisoner, can mislead any single agent; defences are cross-modality consistency checks (P1), DT plausibility filters (P2) and signed anchor updates (P3). The anchor and CTI data space must also outlive “harvest now, decrypt later” attacks, motivating NIST post-quantum cryptography for ledger and STIX/TAXII transport.

Sovereignty and policy compliance. CER/NIS2/AI-Act conformance requires locally hosted open-weight LLMs, strict data residency and explicit human-in-the-loop checkpoints on high-impact actions [12, 13]; the challenge is to codify these inside the SOAR playbook generator rather than as a post-hoc audit [5, 4].

VII Conclusion

RESILAGENT positions Sensing & Data Intelligence, Resilience Analytics & Reporting and Incident Response & Recovery as three sides of one EPES resilience loop fused by agentic AI, real-time DTs and a blockchain anchor. The contribution is not another detection model but an operational architecture that integrates cyber, physical and environmental signals, drives a twin-based decision surface, and produces verifiable CER/NIS2 evidence by design, staged around four irreducible technologies (Sec. III-A) with the rest as extensions. Result 6 runs the full EWS→\toDT→\todetector→\tovision→\toLLM→\toblockchain chain end-to-end with a real Llama-3 agent, the decision path completing in ∼17{\sim}17 s, matched to the human-in-the-loop budget. The evidence does not yet validate closed-loop performance on real operator telemetry, imagery or a production ledger. A national TSO and a parallel DSO pilot will close these gaps; the next steps replace the three proxy components, (F1) the detector and DT wrapped as tools inside a LangGraph agent fed an LLM-parsed Suricata/Wazuh stream, (F2) a multimodal LLM (LLaVA-class) benchmarked on Sentinel-2 and drone imagery against a vision-blind baseline, and (F3) the Open-Meteo demo replaced by the HYDS ARGOS multi-hazard EWS.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
